title: Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty: Beyond OOD Detection and Active Learning
claim: Evaluation tasks rank the same methods very differently, so the choice of downstream task determines which uncertainty estimator looks best.
layout: 2 panels, left rank heatmap and right triangular correlation matrix, hatched diagonal
description: Two heatmap panels. Panel (a) is a table with 14 uncertainty methods as rows (Evidential, BatchEnsemble, SWAG, Deep Ensemble, and others, down to NatPN). Columns are grouped by task: OOD (near, far), AL, Selective prediction (log, Brier, 0/1) and Regret (log, Brier, 0/1). The Regret group is boxed in bold. Each cell holds the method's rank from 1 to 14, colored on a blue (best) to red (worst) diverging scale. Panel (b) is a lower-triangular matrix of Spearman correlations between the task rankings. It uses the same task grouping on both axes, and the Regret block is outlined in black. Diagonal cells are hatched and show the correlation between two seeds of the same task, with values near 0.9. Off-diagonal cells are mostly pale, so the tasks agree little. Each panel has its own colorbar. The eye goes first to the colorful rank grid and the boxed Regret columns.
caption: The tasks used to evaluate epistemic uncertainty disagree on which method is best. Uncertainty quantification methods on CIFAR-10H, each scored by its epistemic estimate. (a) Rank of each method by each task's metric ([ref]). (b) Spearman correlation between the rankings of two tasks; on the hatched diagonal, of two seeds of the same task. The regret task ranks the methods largely unlike OOD detection and active learning, while each task's ranking is stable across seeds.
abstract: Current evaluation of epistemic uncertainty relies on tasks such as out-of-distribution detection, active learning and selective prediction. However, common epistemic uncertainty scores, such as mutual information or the variance of the predictions, estimate the regret, the excess error of a predictor over the Bayes-optimal predictor. Building on the epistemic reject-option framework, we evaluate epistemic uncertainty using its ability to identify regret, and compare this evaluation with the other tasks. Benchmarking standard methods on datasets with repeated human labels reveals that the tasks rank the methods differently, including pairwise rank inversions between methods that are top-ranked on one criterion and bottom-ranked on another. The disagreement is present already at the optimum, where each task calls for a different score. Formulating selective prediction as a constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret, we prove that the optimal score is a convex combination of the ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, so that selective prediction and the regret task are the two endpoints of one family of tasks. Out-of-distribution detection, active learning and the regret task thus disagree, theoretically as well as empirically, on which method is a good estimator of epistemic uncertainty, while selective prediction departs from the regret task where the true risk and the regret order the inputs differently. Researchers must therefore state the downstream decision that an epistemic uncertainty estimate is meant to support, instead of relying on a general notion of model ignorance.
